Brief: Tell me about the Antikythera mechanism and how it was decoded.

1. The Antikythera mechanism ( AN-tik-ih-THEER-ə, US also AN-ty-kih-) is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery (model of the Solar System) built in the 2nd century BC and discovered in 1901.
2. It is the oldest surviving analogue computer discovered to date, although descriptions of similar devices exist in the historical record.
3. It could be used to predict astronomical positions and eclipses decades in advance.
4. It could also be used to track the four-year cycle of athletic games similar to an olympiad, the cycle of the ancient Olympic Games.
5. The artefact was among wreckage retrieved from a shipwreck off the coast of the Greek island Antikythera in 1901.
6. In 1902, during a visit to the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, it was noticed by Greek politician Spyridon Stais as containing a gear, prompting the first study of the fragment by his cousin, Valerios Stais, the museum director.
7. The device, housed in the remains of a wooden-framed case of (uncertain) overall size 34 cm × 18 cm × 9 cm (13.4 in × 7.1 in × 3.5 in), was found as one lump, later separated into three main fragments which are now divided into 82 separate fragments after conservation efforts.
8. Four of these fragments contain gears, while inscriptions are found on many others.
9. The largest gear is about 13 cm (5 in) in diameter and originally had 223 teeth.
10. All these fragments of the mechanism are kept at the National Archaeological Museum, along with reconstructions and replicas, to demonstrate how it may have looked and worked.
11. In 2005, a team from Cardiff University led by Mike Edmunds used computer X-ray tomography and high resolution scanning to image inside fragments of the crust-encased mechanism and read faint inscriptions that once covered the outer casing.
12. This motion was studied in the 2nd century BC by astronomer Hipparchus of Rhodes, and he may have been consulted in the machine's construction.
